title: Blocking and non-blocking code
idea: Blocking code makes the thread wait until its work finishes. Non-blocking code starts the work, returns at once, and handles the result later.
points: Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so one slow call delays everything.
Sync functions, like `readFileSync`, hold that thread until the disk answers.
Async calls hand work off; the event loop (next page) runs your callback later.
`await` pauses only your function; the thread keeps serving other work.

steps.caption: Blocking version. Requests A and B arrive, and each handler calls `readFileSync`.
The thread starts handler A. Request B keeps waiting.
`readFileSync` waits for the disk. The thread can run nothing else, so B stays stuck.
The disk answers and handler A finishes.
Only now can the thread take request B.
B blocks on its own read the same way. B waited for all of A's read.
Result: two reads, strictly one after the other.
Non-blocking version. The same requests arrive, and each handler calls `readFile` with a callback.
`readFile` hands the read to the disk and returns at once. Handler A can finish.
Handler A has returned, so the free thread takes B at once. Both reads now run together.
Say A's read finishes first. Node runs its callback on the free thread.
Then B's callback runs. Nobody waited in line behind a read.

pitfalls: Do not use `readFileSync` while serving requests: one slow read freezes every user.
The result of an async call is available only inside its callback, or after `await`.
A long loop or a huge `JSON.parse` blocks the thread like a sync read.

quiz.why: The callback runs only after the script's sync code finishes, even though `readFile` started first.

takeaway: In a server, use the async version of any call that waits.
